note.text: A shades S-only; E shades overlap; I puts x in overlap; O puts x in S-only. Shading means empty and x means at least one. Blank is unspecified. Keep the existence convention explicit.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to translate between a categorical statement, its A/E/I/O symbol and a correctly marked Venn diagram. Builds on: categorical forms and whole-class coverage. Leads to: clear symbolisation before combining claims in later arguments.

sections.heading: Give the marks a fixed meaning
sections.text: The overlapping circles represent classes S and P. Their overlap contains shared members; S-only contains S outside P. Shading says a region is empty. An x asserts at least one object in a region. An unmarked region is unspecified, not necessarily occupied. Here we use the modern convention: a universal proposition alone adds no existence mark. An explicit existence assumption must be stated if a traditional treatment is used.

sections.heading: Translate each form
sections.text: A, All S are P: shade S-only, because no S may be outside P. E, No S are P: shade the overlap. I, Some S are P: put x in the overlap. O, Some S are not P: put x in S-only. The example diagram shows A. Its blank overlap is not evidence of existence.

sections.heading: Read back to check
sections.text: For an invented Bamenda club, let S be club members and P badge holders. An x in S-only represents a member without a badge, so it is O. Read your completed diagram back into words before accepting it. Changing shading to x reverses empty into occupied; placing the right kind of mark in the wrong region also changes the assertion.

key_words.meaning: an assertion that a region is empty
an assertion of at least one object
members common to S and P

mistake.wrong: Unshaded overlap proves shared members exist.
mistake.why: A universal diagram alone does not add the existence asserted by a particular form.

worked_example.problem: Represent No library books are loanable items with S for books and P for loanable items.
steps: No denies that an object belongs to both classes.
The forbidden region is their overlap.
Shade the overlap; do not place an existence x.

cards.idea: Read the quantifier and copula before choosing a code.
example: A: all are; E: no are; I: some are; O: some are not.

cards.idea: The region and the kind of mark both matter.
example: E: Shade the overlap of S and P.
I: Place x in the overlap.
O: Place x in the S-only region.

cards.idea: Blank regions do not assert existence.
example: The A diagram shades S-only without adding x to the overlap.

questions.prompt: Find the incorrect claim, then read the reason for the correction.

right.explain: This is a correct rule: Shading denotes an empty region. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

right.text: An x asserts at least one object in its region.
right.explain: This is a correct rule: An x asserts at least one object in its region. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

right.text: An unmarked region has unspecified occupancy.
right.explain: This is a correct rule: An unmarked region has unspecified occupancy. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

right.text: An A diagram shades S outside P.
right.explain: This is a correct rule: An A diagram shades S outside P. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

wrong.text: An x proves exactly one object exists in the region.
wrong.explain: It asserts at least one, without an upper bound.

wrong.text: A white unmarked region must contain an object.
wrong.explain: It may be empty or occupied; the diagram has not specified it.

wrong.text: No S are P is represented by x in the overlap.
wrong.explain: That x represents Some S are P; No S are P shades the overlap.

wrong.text: All S are P automatically requires an existence x in the overlap under the stated convention.
wrong.explain: The modern convention shades S-only; it adds no x without an existence premise.
